# distributions3: Probability Distributions as S3 Objects

<!-- badges: start -->
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/distributions3)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=distributions3)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/zeileis/distributions3/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/zeileis/distributions3?branch=main)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/zeileis/distributions3/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/zeileis/distributions3/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

## Features

`distributions3` provides a comprehensive and object-oriented toolbox for probability distributions.

- Distributions are provided as S3 objects. Essentially, these are represented as data
  frames of parameters but with a dedicated class, e.g., `"Normal"`, inheriting from `"distribution"`.
   
- Methods `pdf()` (probability density function or probability mass function), `cdf()`
  (cumulative distribution function), `quantile()` (quantile function, inverse of `cdf()`), and
  `random()` (random samples) replace the d/p/q/r functions provided in base R and many other
  packages such as `dnorm()`, `pnorm()`, `qnorm()`, `rnorm()` for the normal distribution.
   
- Methods for computing central moments via `mean()`, `variance()`, `skewness()`, and `kurtosis()`.

- Methods for extracting the `score()` (first derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the 
  parameters) and `hessian()` (corresponding second derivative.
  
- Numerical fallback implementations for most of these methods in case no dedicated method is
  available for a certain distribution.


## Goals

- User-friendly interface for illustrations in introductory statistics classes and also
  advanced probabilistic modeling and regression courses.

- Developer-friendly interface for fitting and assessing probabilistic models, e.g., via
  [gamlss2](https://gamlss-dev.github.io/gamlss2/) and
  [topmodels](https://zeileis.codeberg.page/topmodels/).


## Installation

The stable version of `distributions3` is available from
[CRAN](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=distributions3):

``` r
install.packages("distributions3")
```

The latest development version can be installed from
[R-universe](https://zeileis.R-universe.dev/distributions3):

``` r
install.packages("distributions3", repos = "https://zeileis.R-universe.dev")
```


## Basic usage

To illustrate the basic usage of `distributions3` we consider two
hypothetical examples for probability distributions:

- Test scores for assessing a person's
  [intelligence quotient (IQ)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_quotient)
  are typically calibrated such that they follow approximately a
  normal distribution with mean 100 and standard deviation 15 in the
  population.

- The goals scored by each team in a soccer match typically
  follow approximately a Poisson distribution whose mean depends on
  the strengths of the team and its opponent.
  [Forecasts of football tournaments](https://www.zeileis.org/news/fifa2026/)
  often predict the means for such Poisson distributions for all
  competing teams and then assess potential courses of the tournament
  by simulation.
  
For both examples the code below first sets up the probability
distribution(s) and then illustrates the most important `distributions3`
methods.  

```{r}
library("distributions3")

## Normal "IQ" distribution
X <- Normal(100, 15)
X

random(X, 5)

pdf(X, 85)
cdf(X, 85)
quantile(X, 0.159)

mean(X)
variance(X)
skewness(X)

## Vector of Poisson "soccer goals" distributions
Y <- Poisson(c(0.8, 1.2, 1.9, 0.5))
Y

random(Y, 5)

pdf(Y, 0:5)
cdf(Y, 0:5)
quantile(Y, 0.5)

mean(Y)
variance(Y)
skewness(Y)
```

## Related work

Various R packages for modeling probability distributions have plugins for `distributions3`
so that it is easy to obtain probabilistic fits or forecasts and employ these for subsequent
computations (quantiles, moments, exceedance probabilities, scoring rules, etc.). In addition
to base R functions such as `lm()`, `glm()`, `arima()`, etc., packages with `distributions3`
support include:

- [gamlss](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=gamlss),
  [gamlss2](https://gamlss-dev.github.io/gamlss2/),
  [bamlss](https://bamlss.org/),
  [mgcv](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=mgcv)
  for various flavors of generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape.

- [pscl](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=pscl) and
  [countreg](https://zeileis.codeberg.page/countreg)
  for a range of popular count data regressions.

- [betareg](https://zeileis.codeberg.page/betareg) and
  [crch](https://zeileis.codeberg.page/crch)
  for several models for limited dependent variables.

Moreover, the following two packages are noteworthy for making extensive use of the
`distributions3` workflow.

- [gamlss2](https://gamlss-dev.github.io/gamlss2/) not only provides distribution objects
  for the _outputs_ (fits and forecats) produced by the fitted model. It sets up family
  objects as _inputs_ providing all infrastructure for fitting complex distributional regression
  models in an object-oriented way.

- [topmodels](https://zeileis.codeberg.page/topmodels) provides unified infrastructure for
  probabilistic models and distributional regressions, e.g., nicely structured probabilistic
  forecasts, residuals, scoring rules, and diagnostic graphics like rootograms, PIT histograms,
  (randomized) quantile residual Q-Q plots, and reliagrams (reliability diagrams).

Finally, for a comprehensive overview of other R packages providing various probability
distribution see the [CRAN Task View](https://CRAN.R-project.org/view=Distributions).
